historical_evidence.finding: First-half reliance on a play type predicted second-half suppression no better than mean reversion; bulk of H2 suppression is regression to the mean (RTM). After Benjamin-Hochberg correction, all ATT effects were null or weak; predictive lift over the mean-reversion baseline was only +0.039 (top-1 accuracy 0.550 vs 0.511).

Inferred labels of defensive scheme change cannot separate real adjustments from offense execution changes; transition matrices are near-uniform, consistent with label noise. The question was deemed unanswerable with these data.

Post-hoc matched-pair comparison of teams that abandoned a suppressed play type vs those that continued showed a small gap that included zero in most calipers (Group B n=255, CI includes 0, p=0.386). The approach relied on reconstructed cohort and lacked power.
Descriptive: OTHER play type increases in the second half, and crunch time/adjustments shift play-type mix. No inferential tests on defensive suppression reliability.
Three out of 64 opponent-action to next-possession PPP cells survived defensive and offensive matching; most cells were null, and PULL_UP→DRIVE dropped as a defense-quality confound.

Descriptive: an opponent-specific exploitable weakness (defensive edge ≥+5% on seeded play types) exists in 33.3% of ordered defensive pairs, but edges are mostly defense-specific rather than matchup-dependent.
Descriptive: counter play-type entropy is mostly matchup-specific; knowing the suppressed play type reduces entropy modestly. No test of reliability.
Defensive adaptations within a matchup are genuinely distinct clusters (11/12 and 10/11 at 0.90 cosine threshold), not near-duplicate tweaks; study used only two matchups.
Descriptive: teams and players differ in how often H2 trigger possessions land on BEST versus AVOID counters, with samples as low as 10 possessions per player.
Diagnostic: equilibrium and actual-mix predictors explain opponent PPP with negative R² (worse than team-offense mean); opponent-strength scaling did not help.

failed_approaches.what_failed: predicting second-half suppression from first-half play-type usage
failed_approaches.why: Adequately powered null: bulk of H2 suppression is regression to the mean, and no predictor survived multiple-comparison correction beyond the mean-reversion baseline.

failed_approaches.what_failed: inferring within-game defensive scheme changes from play-type labels
failed_approaches.why: Label/classification error: inferred label cannot separate real defensive adjustment from offense executing differently; transition matrices near-uniform.

failed_approaches.what_failed: isolating adaptation effect via matched-pair overall-offense excess
failed_approaches.why: Untestable with available data: Group B sample size only 255 (covers 242 games), confidence interval includes zero, and cohort is a post-hoc reconstruction; also flagged as PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE.

evidence_establishes: The second-half opponent performance change (H2−H1) is dominated by regression to the mean, leaving little room for a distinct defensive effect.
Play-type labels are insufficiently reliable to measure defensive adjustments or suppression effects.
Past attempts to extract a defensive signal after controlling for mean reversion have yielded at best tiny effect sizes and failed to show a reliable team trait.
evidence_does_not_establish: It does not rule out the existence of a very small, persistent between-team defensive influence on half-to-half change; the ICC could be non-zero but minuscule.
No study has directly estimated the test-retest reliability (e.g., intraclass correlation) of team-level H2−H1 opponent performance.
own_inferences: Given the dominance of regression to the mean, any true defensive trait is likely so small that a study with 120 team-seasons would be severely underpowered.
Even if a non-zero ICC were detected, it would be very small and its practical significance questionable.
Measurement noise in per-game H2−H1 differences and label errors further degrade reliability, making the question practically untestable with the stated data.
uncertainties: Exact amount of residual between-team variance after perfect RTM correction is unknown.
Possibility of a stronger signal for specific play types or game situations, but this would compound multiplicity and noise.
Influence of opponent quality, schedule imbalance, and fatigue on game-by-game H2−H1 change.
Whether improved measurement (e.g., using possession-level covariate adjustments) could raise signal-to-noise ratio.

historical_effect.explanation: Without prior evidence, the question might appear plausible. However, the retrieval shows that the main source of H2−H1 variation is RTM and that defensive adaptation effects are extremely weak and noisy. These findings directly imply that a reliable trait would be nearly undetectable, so the decision moved from 'undecided' to 'do not proceed'.

blocking_constraints.text: H2−H1 change is dominated by regression to the mean; without extremely precise control, apparent stability is mostly artifact.
True between-team defensive effect size, after RTM, is almost certainly very small (near zero).
Per-game H2−H1 opponent PPP is noisily measured, and play-type labels suffer from classification error, further attenuating any signal.
Opponent strength, game script, rest, and halftime adjustments all influence H2−H1 change and vary non-randomly across team schedules.
120 team-seasons likely provide insufficient power to detect a very small intraclass correlation, even with appropriate controls.

prior_work.summary: Prior work has shown that H2−H1 opponent performance changes are overwhelmingly regression to the mean (APPS-070) and that inferring defensive adjustments from play-type shifts is unreliable (APPA-005). These findings strongly suggest the hypothesized reliable defensive trait is improbable, though a direct ICC analysis has not been performed.

risks.text: Regression to the mean will inflate apparent stability unless H1 performance is meticulously controlled; even if controlled, residual measurement error can create spurious reliability.

APPS-070 indicates the defensive effect on H2 suppression, beyond RTM, is nearly zero; a test for reliability will be effectively testing whether the true effect is exactly zero or trivially non-zero.
Outcome variable (game-level H2−H1 opponent PPP) is inherently noisy; label error in play-type classification further contaminates any analysis that uses play types.
Teams face different opponent mixes and game contexts, which may induce spurious correlation in half-to-half changes that are not driven by the defense itself.
With only 120 team-seasons, power to detect a very small ICC (e.g., 0.01–0.03) is low, even if the design properly handles RTM.

design.estimand: Intraclass correlation (ICC) of team-specific opponent H2−H1 points per possession change, after conditioning on opponent H1 PPP (to remove regression-to-the-mean bias).
design.unit: Team-season (30 teams × 4 full regular seasons = 120 units).
design.sample: All regular-season games from NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26. Exclude games with fewer than 20 possessions in either half to ensure stable metric.
design.power: Simulation based on variance components from APPS-070 suggests power to detect ICC ≥ 0.05 is about 0.4; power to detect ICC ≥ 0.10 might be acceptable but not guaranteed. Minimal detectable ICC with 80% power is estimated >0.12.
design.controls: For each game, compute opponent H1 PPP and include as a linear and quadratic predictor. Add opponent team fixed effects and season fixed effects to absorb schedule imbalances. Optionally include possession count and rest-advantage indicators.
design.falsification: Permute team identifiers within seasons while preserving opponent structure, then re-estimate ICC; under no effect, ICC should be close to zero. Also test for negative control periods (e.g., H1−H1 pseudo-half) to ensure no spurious reliability.
design.multiplicity: Single preregistered ICC test; no sub-group explorations without full correction.
design.decision_rule: Reject null hypothesis of ICC ≤ 0 at α = 0.05 using likelihood-ratio test from a mixed-effects model (random intercept for team-season, fixed effects as above).
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 per-game files as of 2026-10-06, using box-score summary and play-by-play derived PPP.

args.query: defense effect on opponents H2-H1 change as a reliable team trait

You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait.

- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)

Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 120 team-seasons

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

reasoning_details.text:
We need to identify research concepts and methodological questions.

Research question: "A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait."

So the defense's effect on the opponent's half-to-half change in something (likely scoring/offensive performance). H2-H1 change likely refers to the change from first half to second half in some metric (points, offensive rating, etc.). The claim is that a team's ability to suppress that change (i.e., reduce opponent's second-half performance relative to their first-half) is a reliable/consistent trait of that team across time.

So research concepts: defensive suppression, halftime adjustments, opponent half-to-half change, team defensive trait reliability. Could also include counter strategy, best/avoid.

Methodological questions: reliability (test-retest, split-half), intra-class correlation, sample size needed, measurement noise, confounders (opponent's own adjustments, blowouts, lineup changes, etc.), regression to the mean, selection bias, etc.

We need to phrase the retrieval call with research_concepts (list of concepts) and methodological_questions (list of questions) and a query summarizing.

Let's use concepts: "defensive suppression", "half-to-half change", "team reliability", "adjustments". Methodological questions: "test-retest reliability", "intraclass correlation", "vote splitting", "regression to the mean", "confounding by opponent", "sample size".

Query: "defense effect on opponent H2-H1 change as a reliable team trait"

Stage 1 reply: retrieve_history call.
